nodes.text: PagerDuty reports elevated 5xx after the 09:40 deploy wave.
nodes.speaker: Monitor

nodes.text: Open the release war room, assign an incident scribe, and confirm customer impact within five minutes.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

nodes.text: Compare the failing build to the last healthy release and confirm which switch is safest to reverse first.
nodes.speaker: ReleaseEngineer

nodes.text: The feature flag is disabled and the newest requests are draining through the old path.
nodes.speaker: ReleaseEngineer

nodes.text: The previous release is redeploying across the production cluster now.
nodes.speaker: ReleaseEngineer

nodes.text: I am checking replica lag, lock contention, and whether the new schema can safely move backward.
nodes.speaker: Database

nodes.text: Promote the healthy replica, pin writes there, and let the old primary cool down.
nodes.speaker: Database

nodes.text: I have a draft customer update and can publish it as soon as we agree on scope and wording.
nodes.speaker: Comms

nodes.text: Compare trace spans, dependency dashboards, and deploy timing to find out whether the fault sits outside the application pods.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: The vendor bridge is open, and their engineer wants either degraded mode or a five-minute observation window.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: Degraded mode is on, error volume has dropped, and we can check whether the customer-facing path is stable enough to hold.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: Flush the stale cache tier, reload configuration, and watch whether the failing requests clear.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: One region is receiving a bad slice of traffic while the rest of the edge looks healthy.
nodes.speaker: EdgeTeam

nodes.text: The unhealthy zone is drained and user traffic has shifted to the remaining regions.
nodes.speaker: EdgeTeam

nodes.text: Canary routing weights are back to the pre-deploy split.
nodes.speaker: EdgeTeam

nodes.text: Platform engineering is taking over the live mitigation while we preserve notes and customer timelines.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

nodes.text: Keep the release bridge small, assign one owner per hypothesis, and confirm whether the incident is user-visible before escalating.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

nodes.text: I checked the newest pods, recent endpoint changes, and the top failing requests in the service logs.
nodes.speaker: ServiceOwner

nodes.text: The newest pods are restarting, and the previous replicas are still serving traffic.
nodes.speaker: ServiceOwner

nodes.text: Queue depth and worker saturation are the clearest signals, so capacity relief is the fastest next move.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: Extra capacity is online and the backlog is shrinking.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: Noncritical jobs are paused, the backlog is draining, and the hot path has more headroom.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: Customer reports are sparse, but the error budget is burning steadily enough that we may still need to widen the response.
nodes.speaker: SupportLead

nodes.text: Hold a ten-minute watch window and compare live traffic, error budget burn, and support chatter before changing mitigation.
nodes.speaker: Monitor

nodes.text: Check whether the alert came from a synthetic probe, a silenced canary, or a query that changed labels during the deploy.
nodes.speaker: Observability

nodes.text: The alert rule is corrected and historical data confirms that production traffic stayed healthy.
nodes.speaker: Observability

nodes.text: Re-check the core user journey, watch the main dashboards for fifteen minutes, and decide whether the incident is stable enough to close.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

nodes.text: Choose the next review loop based on which hypothesis is still alive after the latest mitigation.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

nodes.text: The incident looks stable, so choose the summary that best matches the mitigation we used and close the loop cleanly.
nodes.speaker: Comms

nodes.text: Close the incident as monitor noise or a self-recovered alert, and attach the query notes for follow-up tuning.
nodes.speaker: Observability

nodes.text: Rollback recovery confirmed, customer traffic is healthy, and the release can stay frozen pending review.
nodes.speaker: Comms

nodes.text: Capacity mitigation held through the watch window, so we can close and schedule scaling follow-up.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

nodes.text: Dependency mitigation is holding, with degraded mode or routing changes documented for the next review.
nodes.speaker: SRE

nodes.text: The feature flag rollback restored stability, and the launch stays disabled until the fix is ready.
nodes.speaker: ReleaseEngineer

nodes.text: Hand off the active mitigation to the next team with timeline, open hypotheses, and customer impact notes attached.
nodes.speaker: IncidentLead

edges.text: 1. [SEV-1] Error rate is above 20% or checkout is fully down.
2. Error rate is elevated but core transactions still succeed.
3. Alert appears noisy or is already recovering.
1. [Rollback] Symptoms started immediately after the latest deploy.
2. [Dependency] Traces point to a gateway, cache, or database dependency.
3. [Comms] Support volume is spiking and a status update may be needed.
1. [Feature Flag] Disable the new feature flag before touching the build.
2. Start a full application rollback.
3. Ask the database owner whether schema changes block a rollback.
1. [DB Failover] Lag or lock contention is severe enough to move traffic.
2. The schema is backward-compatible, so application rollback is safe.
3. We need a specialist on the bridge before changing anything.
1. Publish the customer-facing note and continue dependency triage.
2. Send an internal-only heads-up and continue rollback preparation.
3. Metrics are already improving, so defer the update and re-check stability.
1. [Vendor Escalation] A third-party API latency spike dominates the traces.
2. [Cache Flush] Stale configuration or cache data is serving bad responses.
3. Edge traffic shifted unevenly after the deploy.
4. No external signal stands out, return to the rollback path.
1. Enable degraded mode while the vendor works the incident.
2. Wait five minutes and then repeat dependency checks.
1. Drain the unhealthy zone and keep the remaining regions serving traffic.
2. Revert the canary routing weights to the previous distribution.
3. Escalate the imbalance to the platform war room.
1. [Logs] Errors cluster around one service or endpoint.
2. [Capacity] CPU, memory, or queue depth spiked after rollout.
3. The issue is quiet for customers but persistent in alerts.
1. Restart only the newest pods and keep the rest of the deployment.
2. Disable the new endpoint behind a feature flag.
3. Escalate this to the SEV-1 bridge now.
1. Scale out the workers and web pods.
2. [Queue Drain] Pause noncritical jobs and drain the backlog first.
3. Capacity looks secondary, so inspect dependencies instead.
1. Draft an internal advisory and keep watching the metrics.
2. Escalate to SEV-1 because the burn rate is accelerating.
3. Verify whether this is only monitor noise.
1. Metrics recover during the watch window without another action.
2. Metrics worsen and customer errors start climbing fast.
3. One service keeps failing, so continue service-level checks.
1. The alert only fired from a synthetic probe or silenced canary.
2. The alert query is wrong after a label or dashboard change.
3. We still see uncertain impact, so return to SEV-2 assessment.
1. Metrics are back to baseline and the user journey is healthy.
2. Error rate improved but is not stable enough yet.
3. A second region or service is now impacted.
1. Re-run the service-level checks.
2. Re-run the dependency checks.
3. Prepare a manual handoff to the overnight or platform team.
1. Close this as a rollback recovery.
2. Close this as a capacity recovery.
3. Close this as a dependency mitigation.
4. Close this as a feature-flag mitigation.
